column1: # resolved_modes - POLICY-RESOLVED mode cases
# Format: <expected>\t<label>\t<command>     (TAB separated, exactly 3 columns)
#   expected : ALLOW, WARN or DENY (the Decision line of `dcg explain`)
#   command  : the command line handed to `dcg explain`.
#              A literal \n in this column becomes a real newline.
#              @fixture:<name> loads a multiline command from test/fixtures/.
# Blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored.
# WHY THESE CASES LIVE HERE
# A rule's severity sets its default mode: critical and high deny, medium
# warns, low logs. A WARN goes to stderr and the command runs. The only thing
# that moves a rule between those modes is a `[policy.rules]` entry in
# config.toml. `dcg corpus` applies no policy and records every match as
# "deny", so it cannot see a mode. Before dcg 0.14.4, `dcg explain` reported
# the rule default too, so an explain-based check read DENY while the hook
# let the command through. Each row below pins the resolved mode so a policy
# change in either direction shows up here.
# core.git:stash-drop is severity medium. This policy accepts the default.
# A custom rule cannot harden it: dcg stops at the first matching rule,
# resolves that rule's mode, and never reaches a later critical match.
# stash clear is critical and denies without any override.
WARN
DENY
# core.filesystem:redirect-truncate-dynamic-path is critical by default. The
# `[policy.rules]` entry in example/config.toml relaxes it to WARN, and the
# CI config copies that table, so this row pins the entry itself: dropping it
# from the example turns the row into a DENY.
WARN
